title: 2025-07-02-vetting-to-production-shortlist-roadmapping-demo
summary: Intro demo of Redwood model catalog and bench-to-production path. Covered shortlist creation, benchmark interpretation, compatibility matrix, and routing/fallback options for a production pilot focused on latency-sensitive financial summarization. Agreed to run a 2-week bench with Echelon's prompt set and share quantized variant cost estimates.
topics: Benchmarks: latency, quality, and cost tradeoffs
Compatibility matrix: kernels, quantization, and hardware
Routing and fallback strategies (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
Pilot next steps and data/security questions
action_items: Maya: Share bench template + cost model spreadsheet - due 2025-07-04
Liam: Provision sample bench on Redwood hosted with Echelon prompts (2-week) - due 2025-07-09
Sara: Provide representative prompt set and 1 month of anonymized logs for quality baseline - due 2025-07-07
next_steps: Send security pack (SOC2/ISO summary, SSO options)
Kick off bench with quantized small/medium variants, measure p99 latency and token cost
Follow-up technical deep dive on private deployment if bench meets latency targets
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel, Liam O'Connor (Redwood); Sara Liu, Daniel Brooks, Priya Menon (Echelon Financial)
Links referenced: deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/model-catalog , bench template: https://redwood.ai/bench-templates/echelon-sample , security packet: https://redwood.ai/security-pack.pdf

Summary (auto): quick walkthrough of how to take a shortlist from scouting to a production-ready candidate using Redwood's catalog, bench harness, and compatibility matrix. Discussed tradeoffs for low-latency summarization in finance.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we really appreciate you carving out the time. I'm Maya, I'm the AE on this account, and with me is Liam from engineering who will do most of the demo.
[00:10] Daniel: Hi Maya, Hi Liam, thanks. Sara's going to lead the ML questions, I'm mostly here for timelines and infra constraints.
[00:18] Priya: And I'm looking at how this would slot into our product roadmap.
[00:22] Liam: Great, quick agenda. We'll do a short catalog walkthrough — shortlist creation — then run through our bench results interpretation, the compatibility matrix (kernel/quantization/hardware), and finish with routing and pilot options.
[00:34] Sara: Perfect. Our primary constraint is sub-300ms median and p99 ideally under 700ms for single-document financial summaries. Cost sensitivity is medium; accuracy is high.
[00:45] Liam: Got it. That latency target pushes some choices — small quantized variants are usually our sweet spot. We'll show you the tradeoffs in the bench.
[00:52] [00:52] (brief screen share noise)
[01:05] Liam: Here's the model catalog. You can filter by architecture, tokenization, relative quality, and our perf profile. The shortlist feature lets you pin models and create a bench set.
[01:18] Priya: I like the pinning workflow, can we share that shortlist across teams?
[01:22] Maya: Yes, it's team-shared; links persist and you can export. We'll send the share link after the call.
[01:29] Liam: Clicking into a model we publish a compatibility snapshot — kernel map, supported quantization, typical throughput on our hardware, and an estimated token cost. Note that cost is an estimate based on average sequence length.
[01:44] Sara: We're particularly interested in the kernel map — does Redwood compile different kernels per GPU type?
[01:49] Liam: Yeah, the runtime chooses kernels per architecture and sequence distribution. For many LLMs the attention kernels differ between A100 and H100; we surface that in the matrix so you know which variant to pick.
[01:59] Daniel: Any gotchas with KV cache in quantized models? We've seen regressions with certain 4-bit flows.
[02:05] Liam: Good question. We flag models with known KV cache incompatibilities. Some 4-bit QK variants require an alternative execution path which can add overhead; that's noted in the compat notes.
[02:17] Sara: Could you show an example shortlist for our summarization task?
[02:20] Liam: Sure, I created a quick shortlist: open-llama-13b-q4, redwood-lite-7b-q4, and gnarly-6.7b-fp16 — just as an example set that balances latency and quality.
[02:34] [02:34] Priya: "Gnarly" — is that internal naming?
[02:36] Liam: Apologies naming is messy in the demo environment — that one is a community model we tested.
[02:41] Liam: Next, the bench runner. You upload prompts (or point to S3), choose metrics — we run latency, p99, throughput, and quality via your reference evals. Here's a sample run with your summarized prompts.
[02:55] [03:00] (typing sounds)
[03:12] Liam: Bench results: redwood-lite-7b-q4 has median 210ms, p99 620ms, quality score 0.88 on your ROUGE-style metric. open-llama-13b-q4 is median 320ms, p99 950ms, quality 0.92 — better accuracy but cost and p99 hit. Gnarly-fp16 median 280ms, p99 780ms, quality 0.90.
[03:39] Sara: Those numbers are super useful. The p99 on open-llama is a concern. Is that mostly due to attention kernel differences?
[03:46] Liam: Partially. Also sequence variability. We can run a per-batch sequence-length breakdown if you want to see where the spikes are.
[03:54] Daniel: If we wanted sub-700ms p99, what's the recommendation?
[03:58] Liam: Two paths: pick a smaller quantized model like redwood-lite-7b-q4 and tune batching and KV cache; or go dedicated capacity with H100 and fallback to a cheaper variant — Redwood can route by latency SLO and fall back to cheaper models on overload.
[04:14] Maya: Quick note on private deployments — if you need VPC/on-prem for compliance, we can install the private control plane and still provide the bench tooling. There are tradeoffs on latency headroom depending on your infra.
[04:29] Priya: For compliance we'll need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs.
[04:33] Maya: We support KMS integrations and provide audit log exports. We'll attach the security packet after this call.
[04:40] [04:40] (phone briefly rings in background)
[05:00] Liam: Back to the compatibility matrix — here's how we show kernel mappings across GPU families, and whether a model supports FSDP or sharded execution for larger deployments. That helps you evaluate production cost at scale.
[05:15] Sara: Does Redwood attempt automatic quantization and test it in the bench?
[05:19] Liam: We provide recommended quantization profiles and pre-built variants where available. We can also run a quick quantization pass as part of benching; sometimes community models need separate tuning.
[05:30] Daniel: How do you estimate token cost in the catalog? Is it purely compute time?
[05:34] Liam: We use a combination of GPU cost, memory footprint, and observed throughput from the bench to produce an estimated per-token cost. We'll share the spreadsheet with the formula.
[05:44] Priya: Can we run a bench that simulates peak traffic — like bursty loads during earnings windows?
[05:50] Liam: Yes, bench can simulate your traffic pattern. We'll need representative arrival distributions. The bench runner supports steady-state and burst simulations, and measures tail latency under load.
[06:02] [06:02] (short pause)
[06:10] Sara: Security question — if we send example documents, can Redwood guarantee they won't be used to train models?
[06:16] Maya: Yes, for hosted API we offer a data handling agreement — we don't use customer data to train models unless explicitly opted in. We'll include that language in the security packet.
[06:27] Daniel: Great. On telemetry, we'd like token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route. Does the Console provide that?
[06:33] Liam: Yes Console has per-route dashboards, token-level cost/latency, and traces. You can set alerts on quality regressions tied to prompt sets too.
[06:43] Priya: About routing: you said Redwood can fallback to a cheaper variant. How deterministic is that? We don't want inconsistent outputs for customers.
[06:50] Liam: We support canary and A/B rollouts; fallback can be configured to maintain deterministic variant selection by user or by session. For critical endpoints we recommend a primary/secondary pair with consistent seeding to reduce output drift.
[07:06] Maya: I'll note that we can also pin a specific model version in production for determinism, and roll out changes through a canary.
[07:12] Sara: On benchmarks, how do you score 'quality' — is it ROUGE? Human eval?
[07:18] Liam: You define the metric. We support automated metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, embedding-based similarity) and can integrate human evals. For your summaries we used a ROUGE-L style baseline plus a custom entity-preservation check.
[07:30] [07:30] (keyboard clack)
[07:40] Daniel: Let's talk pilot sizing and cost. If we run a pilot with 200 requests/minute average, what's the expected cost range?
[07:47] Liam: Rough estimate depends on model. For redwood-lite-7b-q4, rough per-token compute cost comes to about $0.0007 per request average (depends on average tokens). We'll create a modeled spreadsheet with your traffic profile.
[08:00] Priya: Can Redwood integrate with our SSO (Okta) and SCIM?
[08:05] Maya: Yes, we support SAML/SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. We'll include setup docs.
[08:12] Sara: Any limitations for PII-heavy inputs? We might need more stringent masking pre-processing.
[08:18] Liam: We can pipeline a preprocessor; or deploy private with customer-managed KMS. We also support redaction hooks.
[08:28] [08:28] (brief overlap chatter)
[08:36] Liam: Demoing the compatibility tab — you can export a CSV for your infra team showing kernel support per GPU, recommended quant, and a boolean for KV cache compatibility.
[08:48] Daniel: Will that CSV align with our cloud provider SKUs (we're on GCP and some on-prem Dell HPE nodes)?
[08:55] Liam: We map to common instance families. For on-prem there may be slight variances; we can run a small micro-benchmark if you provide the node spec.
[09:07] Priya: For the bench run, what's the turnaround?
[09:10] Liam: If we have prompts and an S3 bucket by Monday, we can start the bench and deliver initial results in 5 business days.
[09:17] Sara: That timeline works. We'll anonymize logs and share them.
[09:21] [09:21] Maya: I'll follow up with the bench template and cost model spreadsheet after this meeting.
[09:28] Liam: One more note on fallbacks: Redwood's routing policy can be latency-first (prioritize p99), cost-first, or hybrid. You can also configure region affinity.
[09:40] Daniel: For compliance, do you provide SOC2 Type II reports?
[09:44] Maya: Yes, we have SOC2. We'll send the summary and process for signing an NDA if you need the full report.
[09:52] Priya: Good. Can we get a short technical deep dive next week on private deployment?
[09:57] Maya: Absolutely — shall we propose times in the follow-up?
[10:01] Daniel: Week of July 14th looks good.
[10:05] [10:05] (longer screen-share change)
[10:20] Liam: Back to bench interpretations — here's a cost-quality scatter plot. The red zone shows models that exceed your p99 threshold. You can filter candidates by multiple conditions and the catalog will re-score.
[10:34] Sara: Can we schedule a run that includes a quantization ablation — like Q4 vs Q5 vs FP16?
[10:39] Liam: Yes, bench supports variant ablations. We usually run Q4 and FP16 as baseline; Q5 is experimental depending on the model.
[10:47] Priya: Are there examples of customers who started on hosted then moved to dedicated? Curious about friction.
[10:52] Maya: Several customers started hosted for speed and then reserved Dedicated when they reached predictable volumes; Redwood preserves the model versions and config so transition is smooth. We can share a short case study.
[11:04] [11:04] (small cough)
[11:12] Daniel: If the bench shows quality regressions for quantized variants, do you recommend retraining or just using FP16?
[11:18] Liam: It depends. For small regressions we often tune quantization parameters and use prompt engineering. If it's systemic, FP16 or a larger model may be better.
[11:27] Sara: For the pilot, we'd prefer deterministic outputs for compliance auditing — so pinning is important.
[11:33] Liam: We'll show pinning and canary flows in the deep dive.
[11:38] Maya: Recap and next steps: we'll send bench template, security pack, and modeled cost spreadsheet. Liam will spin up the bench once Sara uploads prompts, and we'll schedule a technical deep dive the week of July 14th.
[11:54] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks!
[11:57] Daniel: Thanks all.
[12:00] Maya: Appreciate your time, talk soon.
[12:05] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional mis-attribution of short utterances; some model names in the demo environment are placeholders.
